extraction_notes.note: theorem (external) or remark: the formal mean-field limit of the cited paper is restated in full but only formally derived there; kept as an external theorem per the cited-result rule.
claim or remark: asserted without argument as a design observation motivating the leave-one-out covariance; kept as claim since DP8 is presented as realising it.

Single sentences introduce several symbols across displayed equations ($C(U)$ and $\bar u$; $m$, $\mathcal C$, $E$; $C_{[j]}$, $\bar u_{[j]}$ and the SDE); sentence rules forbid splitting, so each is one definition node with its numbered equations nested.
Abstract claims (restated by LP1, ClP3, ClP5), the pointer to Propositions 2, 4 and 7 of the cited paper, the remark on [LMW18], and the acknowledgement were not given nodes.
The align in the proof of Lemma 2.1 prints three numbers (13)-(15) but is one environment fact; emitted as one equation node.

nodes.statement: Let us consider a one-dimensional Gaussian target measure (d=1) with variance b^2, i.e. the potential is given by Psi_R(u) = u^2/(2b^2). Under the approximating assumptions that the equilibrium density associated to is a product of J Gaussians with variance sigma^2, and that the covariance at equilibrium can be well-approximated by the state-independent stationary covariance (mean-field assumption), one can derive the relation sigma^2 approx fracJ-2J b^2, which we numerically verified for J=4. Note that sigma^2 < b^2, i.e. the dynamics systematically underestimates the posterior variance. Since sigma^2 xrightarrowJ rightarrow infty b^2, this error vanishes in the large-particle regime, in agreement with the results in .

nodes.statement: This follows from standard arguments for the classical Fokker--Planck equation . See also Proposition 2 of . Let us also mention that the convexity requirement on Psi_R can be relaxed by a perturbation argument due to Holley–-Stroock . The need for a correction term in () can be avoided by ensuring that the jth block entry C(U) in S(U) does not depend on the jth particle position u^(j). This can, for example, be achieved by defining the following modified covariance matrices C_[j](U) = frac1J-1 sum_knot=j (u^(k)-baru_[j])(u^(k)-bar u_[j])^T in R^dtimes d, j=1,ldots,J, where bar u_[j] denotes the leave-one-out sample mean bar u_[j] = frac1J-1sum_knot=j^J u^(k), and by replacing () with dotu^(j) = -C_[j](U)nabla Psi_R(u^(j)) + sqrt2C_[j](U) dotW^(j). We note that very similar ideas have been employed, for example, in for second-order Langevin dynamics. However, while the reformulation () is appealing, its computational implementation is more demanding due to the need for computing J different covariance matrices and their square roots. On the other hand, if the destabilising effect of the correction term in () leads to numerical difficulties under small or moderate particle sizes, then () could be taken as a starting point for formulating gradient-free formulations in the spirit of the ensemble Kalman sampler (EKS) as proposed in .
nodes.raw_latex:
This follows from standard arguments for the classical Fokker--Planck equation
\cite{sr:P14}. See also Proposition 2 of \cite{sr:GIHLS19}. Let us also mention that the convexity requirement on $\Psi_R$ can be relaxed by a perturbation argument due to Holley–-Stroock \cite{sr:P14}. 

The need for a correction term in (\ref{eq:IPS1}) can be avoided by ensuring that the $j$th block entry $C(U)$ in $S(U)$ 
does not depend on the $j$th particle position $u^{(j)}$. This can, for example, be achieved by defining the following modified 
covariance matrices
\begin{equation}
C_{[j]}(U) = \frac{1}{J-1} \sum_{k\not=j} (u^{(k)}-\bar{u}_{[j]})(u^{(k)}-\bar u_{[j]})^{\rm T} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, \quad j=1,\ldots,J, 
\end{equation}
where $\bar u_{[j]}$ denotes the leave-one-out sample mean
\begin{equation}
\bar u_{[j]} = \frac{1}{J-1}\sum_{k\not=j}^J u^{(k)},
\end{equation}
and by replacing (\ref{eq:IPS1}) with
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IPS3}
\dot{u}^{(j)} = -C_{[j]}(U)\nabla \Psi_R(u^{(j)}) + \sqrt{2C_{[j]}(U)} \dot{\bf W}^{(j)}.
\end{equation}
We note that very similar ideas have been employed, for example, in \cite{sr:LMW18} for second-order Langevin dynamics. However, while
the reformulation (\ref{eq:IPS3}) is appealing, its computational implementation is more demanding due to the need for computing $J$ 
different covariance matrices and their square roots.  On the other hand, if the destabilising
effect of the correction term in (\ref{eq:IPS1c}) leads to numerical difficulties under small or moderate particle sizes, 
then (\ref{eq:IPS3}) could be taken as a starting point for formulating gradient-free formulations in the spirit of the ensemble Kalman 
sampler (EKS) as proposed in \cite{sr:GIHLS19}.
